Let $P=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$ be the polynomial algebra whose elements involve finitely many indeterminates, as in [[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]. Give $x_r$ degree $r$ and write $P_d$ for its degree-$d$ subspace. On $P$, put

$$a_{-r}=x_r\cdot,\qquad a_r=r\frac{\partial}{\partial x_r}\quad(r\ge1),\qquad a_0=0,\qquad \mathbf1=1,\qquad T=\sum_{r\ge1}r x_{r+1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_r}.$$

Every sum of operators here is applied to a polynomial and is then finite. Define $a(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nz^{-n-1}$, in the conventions of [[def-formal-distribution-on-a-vector-space]], and the divided derivative $b_r(z)=\partial_z^{r-1}a(z)/(r-1)!$ for $r\ge1$. In normal ordering, all modes $a_n$ with $n<0$ are moved to the left of all modes with $n\ge0$, preserving their respective internal orders. For a polynomial monomial $v=x_{r_1}\cdots x_{r_s}$ define the candidate field

$$Y(v,z)={:}b_{r_1}(z)\cdots b_{r_s}(z){:},\qquad Y(1,z)=I.$$

The empty normal product is the identity. The same-sign modes commute, so the formula is symmetric in the listed factors; it is extended linearly from the polynomial monomial basis. Set $\omega=\tfrac12 x_1^2$. The well-defined state-field and conformal-VOA structure on this vacuum space are proved in [[thm-rank-one-heisenberg-vertex-operator-algebra]]. The symbol $a_n$ is a current mode; in particular $Y(x_1,z)=a(z)$ and $Y(\omega,z)=\sum_nL(n)z^{-n-2}$ use different mode shifts.

Let $V$ be a complex vector space. A **formal distribution** in variables $z,w$ with coefficients in a complex vector space $E$ is an arbitrary coefficient family
$$F(z,w)=\sum_{p,q\in\mathbb Z}F_{p,q}z^pw^q,\qquad F_{p,q}\in E.$$
No convergence or summability is assumed. Multiplication by a polynomial in $z,w$ is defined coefficientwise; each resulting coefficient is a finite sum. The residue $\operatorname{Res}_z F$ is the coefficient of $z^{-1}$, retaining the other variables and coefficients. For a one-variable series $f(z)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}f_mz^m$, write $\operatorname{Res}_z f=f_{-1}$, in the same support convention as [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]].

The **formal delta distribution** is
$$\delta(z,w)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}z^{-n-1}w^n.$$
For each integer $r$, the two binomial expansions of $(z-w)^r$ are
$$\iota_{z,w}(z-w)^r=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom rj(-1)^jz^{r-j}w^j,\qquad \iota_{w,z}(z-w)^r=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom rjz^j(-w)^{r-j},$$
where $\binom rj=r(r-1)\cdots(r-j+1)/j!$ and $\binom r0=1$. The first expansion is in nonnegative powers of $w$ and the second is in nonnegative powers of $z$; they are distinct when $r<0$.

A formal distribution $A(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_nz^{-n-1}$ with $A_n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ is a **field on $V$** if for every $v\in V$ there is an integer $N(v,A)$ such that $A_nv=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,A)$. Equivalently, $A(z)v\in V((z))$: its powers of $z$ are bounded below, as in [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]], with coefficients in $V$. Define its modes by $A_{(n)}=A_n=\operatorname{Res}_z z^nA(z)$.

Two fields $A(z),B(w)$ are **mutually local** if some integer $N\ge0$ satisfies $(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0$ as a formal distribution, where $[A(z),B(w)]=A(z)B(w)-B(w)A(z)$. For any integer $n$, their **$n$th product field** is
$$A(z)_{(n)}B(z)=\operatorname{Res}_x\Bigl(\iota_{x,z}(x-z)^nA(x)B(z)-\iota_{z,x}(x-z)^nB(z)A(x)\Bigr).$$
These conventions use ordinary, ungraded vector spaces and ordinary commutators; no super sign is implicit.

A **conformal vertex algebra of CFT type** is a complex vertex algebra $V$ in the sense of [[def-vertex-algebra-state-field]], with a specified vector $\omega\in V$ and scalar $c\in\mathbb C$, such that, writing
$$
Y(\omega,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}L(n)z^{-n-2},
$$
the operators $L(n)$ and scalar central action $c$ satisfy the Virasoro relations of [[def-virasoro-algebra]], and $L(-1)=T$. In addition, $L(0)$ is diagonalizable, $V_n:=\{v\in V:L(0)v=nv\}$ gives $V=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}V_n$, every $V_n$ is finite dimensional, and $V_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$. Under this page's convention, this is a vertex operator algebra of CFT type. The grading and the CFT-type condition are part of the definition; they do not follow from the vertex-algebra axioms alone.

The conformal weight of $v\in V_n$ is $n$. A conformal vector, a grading, and the nonnegative grading condition are additional data beyond an ordinary vertex algebra.

A (non-super) **vertex algebra** over $\mathbb C$ is a complex vector space $V$ equipped with a nonzero vector $\mathbf1\in V$, a linear operator $T:V\to V$, and a linear **state–field map**
$$Y(-,z):V\longrightarrow (\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V))^{\mathbb Z},\qquad a\longmapsto Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1},$$
where the codomain denotes all endomorphism-valued coefficient families indexed by $\mathbb Z$.
satisfying the following axioms.

1. **Field and truncation.** For each $a,v\in V$, there is an integer $N(a,v)$ such that $a_{(n)}v=0$ for all $n\ge N(a,v)$. Thus $Y(a,z)v\in V((z))$ in the lower-bounded support sense of [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]].

2. **Vacuum and creation.** $Y(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_V$, $T\mathbf1=0$, and
   $$Y(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a:=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{z^rT^r a}{r!}.$$
   This is a formal power series; no analytic convergence is asserted.

3. **Translation covariance.** For every $a\in V$,
   $$[T,Y(a,z)]=\partial_zY(a,z).$$

4. **Locality.** For every $a,b\in V$, some integer $N\ge0$ satisfies
   $$(z-w)^N[Y(a,z),Y(b,w)]=0.$$

The coefficient $a_{(n)}b$ is called the $n$th product of the states $a,b$. The mode and formal-distribution conventions in [[def-formal-distribution-on-a-vector-space]] are in force. The axioms are algebraic and do not impose a grading, conformal vector, simplicity, unitarity, or analytic OPE convergence.

derivations.claim: On every polynomial, differentiation and multiplication give $[a_m,a_n]=m\delta_{m,-n}I$. All sufficiently large positive modes kill that polynomial. Thus $a(z)$ is a field, and its commutator is $\partial_w\delta(z,w)$, obtained by summing $m z^{-m-1}w^{m-1}$. Multiplying this distribution by $(z-w)^2$ gives zero (differentiate $(z-w)\delta(z,w)=0$), so the generator is local with itself. Directly $[T,a_n]=-n a_{n-1}$ and $T1=0$. Also $a(z)1=\sum_{r\ge1}x_rz^{r-1}=e^{zT}x_1$, since $T^j x_1=j!x_{j+1}$. The negative modes are the multiplication operators $x_r$, whose monomials span $P$. All hypotheses of [F2] hold.

The reconstruction has precisely the stated normal fields. Indeed the two binomial expansions in [F3], with index $-r$, give $a(z)_{(-r)}B(z)={:}b_r(z)B(z){:}$: taking the residue separates the modes $a_{-r-j}$, with coefficient $\binom{r+j-1}{j}z^j$, from the modes $a_j$, with coefficient $(-1)^{r-1}\binom{r+j-1}{j}z^{-r-j}$. These are the divided derivatives of the negative and nonnegative parts of $a$. By [F2]'s vacuum-state transport, the state of that product is $a_{-r}v=x_rv$ if $B=Y(v,z)$. Induction on the number of factors gives the displayed monomial formula. The same-sign modes commute, so nesting these normal products introduces no extra contractions. This proves the candidate state fields coincide with the reconstructed ones.

Since $Y(\omega,z)=\tfrac12{:}a(z)^2{:}$, its coefficient is the quadratic sum stated. For a fixed $n$ and polynomial, only finitely many terms survive: modes of large positive index kill the polynomial after normal ordering, and the sum of two negative indices is fixed. The oscillator commutator gives $[L(n),a_m]=-m a_{n+m}$ by the two terms $k=-m$ and $n-k=-m$ in that sum. Directly the sums at $n=0,-1$ give $L(0)=\sum_{r\ge1}a_{-r}a_r$ and $L(-1)=\sum_{r\ge1}a_{-r-1}a_r=T$, since $a_0=0$.

Let $C_{m,n}=[L(m),L(n)]-(m-n)L(m+n)$. Step 3.1 and the operator commutator identity show that $C_{m,n}$ commutes with every $a_r$. Any operator commuting with all multiplication operators and all positive derivatives is scalar: its value on $1$ is killed by every partial derivative and hence is constant, and commuting with multiplication determines its value on every monomial. Each $L(n)$ has degree $-n$, so this scalar is zero unless $m+n=0$. For $m>0$, $L(m)1=L(0)1=0$ and $L(-m)1=\tfrac12\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}x_r x_{m-r}$. Applying $L(m)$ with step 3.1 gives $C_{m,-m}1=\tfrac12\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}r(m-r)1=(m^3-m)1/12$. Antisymmetry covers negative $m$, and $m=0$ is zero. Thus $[L(m),L(n)]=(m-n)L(m+n)+(m^3-m)\delta_{m,-n}I/12$.

The explicit Euler operator in step 3.1 has weight $d$ on $P_d$. For fixed $d$, only $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ can occur, with $m_r\le d/r$, so its monomial basis is finite. There are no negative degrees, and degree zero consists of constants. Along with $L(-1)=T$ and the Virasoro relations of step 4.1, these verify every requirement in [F4]. No choice principle or analytic completion is used.

The data in [[def-rank-one-heisenberg-vertex-algebra]] define a vertex algebra with the displayed normal-monomial state fields. $$L(n)=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}{:}a_k a_{n-k}{:},\qquad L(0)=\sum_{r\ge1}r x_r\frac{\partial}{\partial x_r},\qquad L(-1)=T.$$

Each quadratic-mode sum is finite on every vector. The weight-$d$ space is $P_d$, with the finite basis of monomials $\prod_r x_r^{m_r}$ satisfying $\sum_r r m_r=d$; in particular $P_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$.

Let $V$ be a complex vector space. A **formal distribution** in variables $z,w$ with coefficients in a complex vector space $E$ is an arbitrary coefficient family
$$F(z,w)=\sum_{p,q\in\mathbb Z}F_{p,q}z^pw^q,\qquad F_{p,q}\in E.$$

where $\binom rj=r(r-1)\cdots(r-j+1)/j!$ and $\binom r0=1$. The first expansion is in nonnegative powers of $w$ and the second is in nonnegative powers of $z$; they are distinct when $r<0$.

These conventions use ordinary, ungraded vector spaces and ordinary commutators; no super sign is implicit.

With the two-variable formal delta distribution and binomial expansions of [[def-formal-distribution-on-a-vector-space]],
$$
z_0^{-1}\delta\!\left(\frac{z_1-z_2}{z_0}\right)-z_0^{-1}\delta\!\left(\frac{z_2-z_1}{-z_0}\right)=z_2^{-1}\delta\!\left(\frac{z_1-z_0}{z_2}\right),
$$
where the first term expands in nonnegative powers of $z_2$, the second in nonnegative powers of $z_1$, and the right side in nonnegative powers of $z_0$.

Let $V$ be a vertex algebra over $\mathbb C$ in the ordinary, non-super convention of [[def-vertex-algebra-state-field]]. A **left $V$-module** is a complex vector space $M$ and a linear map
$$
Y_M(-,z):V\longrightarrow \{\text{formal fields on }M\},\qquad a\longmapsto Y_M(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a^M_{(n)}z^{-n-1},
$$
with the following properties:

1. **Lower truncation.** For every $a\in V$ and $m\in M$, $a^M_{(n)}m=0$ for all sufficiently large integers $n$, so $Y_M(a,z)m\in M((z))$ in the support convention of [[def-formal-distribution-on-a-vector-space]].

2. **Vacuum.** $Y_M(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_M$.

3. **Module Jacobi identity.** For every $a,b\in V$,
$$
z_0^{-1}\delta\!\left(\frac{z_1-z_2}{z_0}\right)Y_M(a,z_1)Y_M(b,z_2)-z_0^{-1}\delta\!\left(\frac{z_2-z_1}{-z_0}\right)Y_M(b,z_2)Y_M(a,z_1)=z_2^{-1}\delta\!\left(\frac{z_1-z_0}{z_2}\right)Y_M(Y(a,z_0)b,z_2).
$$
Here $\delta(x)=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}x^r$; the first expansion is in nonnegative powers of $z_2$, the second in nonnegative powers of $z_1$, and the right-hand expansion is in nonnegative powers of $z_0$. They use the formal binomial conventions of [[def-formal-distribution-on-a-vector-space]]. The $Y$ inside the right-hand side is the state-field map of $V$; it is not the action map $Y_M$.

A **$V$-module homomorphism** $f:M\to N$ is a linear map such that $fY_M(a,z)=Y_N(a,z)f$ for every $a\in V$. This definition does not impose a conformal grading, finite-dimensional weight spaces, semisimplicity of $L_0$, a right-module convention, or a twist by an automorphism. For a conformal vertex algebra, write $Y_M(\omega,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}L_M(n)z^{-n-2}$ when a conformal vector $\omega$ is specified.

A **$V$-submodule** of $M$ is a linear subspace stable under every mode $a^M_{(n)}$. A module is **simple** (or **irreducible**) if it is nonzero and has no proper nonzero $V$-submodule. A module is **completely reducible** (or **semisimple**) if it is an internal direct sum of simple $V$-submodules; the empty direct sum is the zero module.

Let $V=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}V_r$ be a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type and $M$ a left $V$-module. The module is **admissible** if it is equipped with a direct-sum grading $M=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}M(n)$ such that for every homogeneous $a\in V_r$, every integer mode $k$, and every $n\ge0$,
$$
a^M_{(k)}M(n)\subseteq M(n+r-k-1),
$$
where $M(q)=0$ for $q<0$. No diagonalizability of $L_M(0)$ is required: the conformal mode $L_M(0)=\omega^M_{(1)}$ preserves each $M(n)$, but may act there nonsemisimply. In this definition, morphisms preserve the specified nonnegative grading and commute with every module field.

derivations.claim: The polynomial formulas give $[a_m,a_n]=m\delta_{m,-n}I$ on $F(E,A)$: the zero mode commutes with every mode because it acts on $E$ alone. Every positive mode of index exceeding the degree of a polynomial kills it. In a fixed coefficient of a normal product applied to a degree-$d$ vector, all nonnegative modes act first. Their positive indices have bounded total sum, at most $d$; there are finitely many such choices, including zero indices. The total exponent then bounds the sum of the remaining negative indices, so there are finitely many remaining choices too. Every coefficient is therefore a genuine endomorphism. Counting degrees in a term of $b_r^F(z)$ gives degree change $-n$ at exponent $-n-r$. For a weight-$w$ monomial, $w=\sum r_i$, so its coefficient of $z^{-k-1}$ has degree change $w-k-1$. This proves the displayed shift and lower truncation; $Y_F(1,z)=I$ is the vacuum action.

The delta identity [F3] implies, for each scalar Laurent monomial $z^r w^s(z-w)^{-K}$ with $K\ge0$, the corresponding identity $D_{12}\iota_{z,w}G-D_{21}\iota_{w,z}G=D_{20}\iota_{w,z_0}G(w+z_0,w)$. Indeed multiplying either of the first two delta sums by its expansion of $(z-w)^{-K}$ shifts the delta summation index and gives $z_0^{-K}$ times that delta sum. Also $D_{20}z=D_{20}(w+z_0)$, directly from its delta sum; integer powers give substitution of $z^r$, using the binomial inverse of $w+z_0$ for negative $r$. Multiplying [F3] by $z^r w^s z_0^{-K}$ therefore gives exactly the asserted identity, with the prescribed expansions.

Split $a^F=a^-+a^+$ into $n<0$ and $n\ge0$. The only mixed commutator is $[a^+(z),a^-(w)]=\sum_{n\ge1}n z^{-n-1}w^{n-1}=\iota_{z,w}(z-w)^{-2}I$; same-sign parts commute. Differentiating gives the scalar contraction $K_{r,s}(z-w)=(-1)^{r-1}(r+s-1)!\,(z-w)^{-r-s}/((r-1)!(s-1)!)$ for $b_r^F(z),b_s^F(w)$. For $u=\prod_{i=1}^p x_{r_i}$ and $v=\prod_{j=1}^q x_{s_j}$, let a partial matching $J$ pair distinct left factors with distinct right factors, and write $I(J),O(J)$ for its unmatched left and right indices. Define the common expression $G_F(z,w)=\sum_J(\prod_{(i,j)\in J}K_{r_i,s_j}(z-w)){:}\prod_{i\in I(J)}b_{r_i}^F(z)\prod_{j\in O(J)}b_{s_j}^F(w){:}$. This is a finite sum over matchings. Reorder the annihilators of the left product across the creators of the right product. At each crossing use $XY=YX+[X,Y]$; every commutator is the displayed scalar and commutes with all remaining factors. Each choice of disjoint crossings contributes exactly one partial matching, including the empty matching. This proves $Y_F(u,z)Y_F(v,w)=\iota_{z,w}G_F(z,w)$. Reversing the ordered products gives $Y_F(v,w)Y_F(u,z)=\iota_{w,z}G_F(z,w)$: differentiation of $(w-z)^{-2}$ gives the same rational $K_{r_i,s_j}(z-w)$ after swapping variables, and the unmatched normal product is unchanged.

The same calculation on the vacuum space computes every state coefficient $u_{(n)}v$. Apply its Wick expression to $1$ and set $w=0$. This is legitimate because $Y(v,w)1$ has only nonnegative powers of $w$. All nonnegative oscillator modes in the normal product kill $1$, and the negative part of $b_r(z)$ is $\sum_{k\ge0}\binom{r+k-1}{k}x_{r+k}z^k$. Consequently $Y(u,z_0)v$ is the state-valued Laurent series $\sum_J(\prod_{(i,j)\in J}K_{r_i,s_j}(z_0))(\prod_{i\in I(J)}\sum_{k\ge0}\binom{r_i+k-1}{k}x_{r_i+k}z_0^k)(\prod_{j\in O(J)}x_{s_j})$. Every coefficient is a finite sum, since the contraction pole order is bounded and the required sum of the $k$'s is fixed. Apply $Y_F(-,w)$ coefficientwise. The formal Taylor identity $b_r^F(w+z_0)=\sum_{k\ge0}\binom{r+k-1}{k}z_0^k b_{r+k}^F(w)$ follows by differentiating the binomial expansion of each power of $w$. The normal parts obey that same Taylor identity. Hence the resulting iterate is precisely $Y_F(Y(u,z_0)v,w)=\iota_{w,z_0}G_F(w+z_0,w)$. This proves the complete iterate formula, including negative products, rather than only the singular OPE.

Apply step 1.2 termwise to the common expression in step 2.1. To justify every infinite-series operation, fix an input polynomial degree and project the output to degrees at most $D$. Each unmatched normal product then has only finitely many modes in each variable: the positive indices are bounded by the input degree, and the creation indices are bounded by the output degree plus the input degree. It is therefore a Laurent polynomial after this projection, multiplied by the finite-order contraction poles. Step 1.2 applies without an infinite rearrangement. Since $D$ is arbitrary and every vector is a finite sum of homogeneous polynomials, the identity holds coefficientwise on all of $F(E,A)$. Substitute the two ordered products from step 2.1 and the iterate from step 3.1. The resulting equality is exactly the full module Jacobi identity in [F4], for all monomial states and thus all states by linearity. Along with step 1.1 this proves the module assertion. All calculations are algebraic and choice-free.

Let $V=P$ be the rank-one Heisenberg vertex algebra of [[thm-rank-one-heisenberg-vertex-operator-algebra]]. For any complex vector space $E$ and any $A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(E)$, set $F(E,A)=P\otimes E$ and define

$$a_{-r}=x_r\cdot\otimes I_E,\qquad a_r=r\partial_{x_r}\otimes I_E\ (r\ge1),\qquad a_0=I_P\otimes A.$$

Write $a^F(z)=\sum_na_nz^{-n-1}$ and $b_r^F(z)=\partial_z^{r-1}a^F(z)/(r-1)!$. With the same negative/nonnegative-mode normal ordering as [[def-rank-one-heisenberg-vertex-algebra]], put

$$Y_F(x_{r_1}\cdots x_{r_s},z)={:}b_{r_1}^F(z)\cdots b_{r_s}^F(z){:},\qquad Y_F(1,z)=I.$$

These fields give a $V$-module in the full formal-Jacobi convention of [[def-vertex-algebra-module]]. In particular, no diagonalizability or nilpotence condition on $A$ is required. For $v\in P_w$ and $f\in P_d\otimes E$, each mode satisfies

$$v^F_{(k)}f\in P_{d+w-k-1}\otimes E,$$

where negative degrees are zero. Thus the fields are lower truncated, and this is an admissible nonnegative integer grading whenever the module is viewed over the conformal VOA. No logarithmic powers occur in $Y_F$ itself.

The data in [[def-rank-one-heisenberg-vertex-algebra]] define a vertex algebra with the displayed normal-monomial state fields. With $\omega=\tfrac12x_1^2$ it is a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type in the convention of [[def-conformal-vertex-algebra]], with central charge $1$. Its conformal modes are

$$L(n)=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}{:}a_k a_{n-k}{:},\qquad L(0)=\sum_{r\ge1}r x_r\frac{\partial}{\partial x_r},\qquad L(-1)=T.$$

Each quadratic-mode sum is finite on every vector. The weight-$d$ space is $P_d$, with the finite basis of monomials $\prod_r x_r^{m_r}$ satisfying $\sum_r r m_r=d$; in particular $P_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$.

Let $V=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}V_r$ be a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type and $M$ a left $V$-module. The module is **admissible** if it is equipped with a direct-sum grading $M=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}M(n)$ such that for every homogeneous $a\in V_r$, every integer mode $k$, and every $n\ge0$,
$$
a^M_{(k)}M(n)\subseteq M(n+r-k-1),
$$
where $M(q)=0$ for $q<0$. No diagonalizability of $L_M(0)$ is required: the conformal mode $L_M(0)=\omega^M_{(1)}$ preserves each $M(n)$, but may act there nonsemisimply. In this definition, morphisms preserve the specified nonnegative grading and commute with every module field.

Let $V$ be a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type and $M$ a left $V$-module. Write $L_M(0)$ for the coefficient determined by
$$
Y_M(\omega,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}L_M(n)z^{-n-2}.
$$
For $h\in\mathbb C$, define the generalized $L_M(0)$-eigenspace
$$
M_{[h]}=\{m\in M:(L_M(0)-h)^N m=0\text{ for some integer }N\ge1\}.
$$
The module is **grading-restricted generalized** if $M=\bigoplus_{h\in\mathbb C}M_{[h]}$, every $M_{[h]}$ is finite dimensional, and the real parts of its nonzero generalized weights are bounded below. The direct sum means each vector has only finitely many generalized-weight components. This convention explicitly adds finite-dimensionality and a lower bound to the generalized-eigenspace decomposition; those conditions are not consequences of the module Jacobi identity.

A **logarithmic module** for a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type is a grading-restricted generalized module, as in [[def-grading-restricted-generalized-vertex-module]], on which $L_M(0)$ is not semisimple. Equivalently, some generalized weight space contains $m$ and $h\in\mathbb C$ with $(L_M(0)-h)^r m=0$ and $(L_M(0)-h)^{r-1}m\ne0$ for an integer $r\ge2$. This definition records the Jordan-block condition; it does not assert that a named vertex algebra has such a module or that its module category has any particular tensor, finite-length, or modular property.

An **ordinary module** for a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type is a grading-restricted generalized module in the sense of [[def-grading-restricted-generalized-vertex-module]] on which $L_M(0)$ acts semisimply. Equivalently, $M$ is a direct sum of its ordinary eigenspaces $M_h=\{m:L_M(0)m=hm\}$, each eigenspace is finite dimensional, and the real parts of the occurring weights are bounded below. Ordinary-module status is a condition on the module action; it does not assert that the category of such modules is semisimple.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] with the displayed $E,A_\lambda$. This already gives a genuine module with all three-variable Jacobi coefficients verified, not merely a representation of the current-mode Lie algebra. Formula [F2] and the action definition give $Y_F(\omega,z)=\tfrac12{:}a^F(z)^2{:}$, so its modes are the displayed quadratic sums, finite on each polynomial vector by the same normal-order bounds as [F1]. At $n=0$ this gives $L_F(0)=\sum_{r\ge1}a_{-r}a_r+a_0^2/2=D\otimes I+A_\lambda^2/2$. Since $N^2=0$, $A_\lambda^2/2=(\lambda^2/2)I+\lambda N$.

The conformal modes also satisfy the central-charge-one Virasoro relations directly. The oscillator commutator gives $[L_F(n),a_m]=-m a_{n+m}$. Thus $C_{m,n}=[L_F(m),L_F(n)]-(m-n)L_F(m+n)$ commutes with every multiplication and derivative mode and is determined by its action on the common positive-mode kernel $E$. Its degree is $-m-n$; an operator commuting with all positive modes must send $E$ into $E$, so $C_{m,n}|_E=0$ if $m+n\ne0$. For $m>0$, $L_F(m)E=0$ and $L_F(-m)e=x_m A_\lambda e+\tfrac12\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}x_r x_{m-r}e$. Applying $L_F(m)$ gives $m A_\lambda^2e+\tfrac12\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}r(m-r)e$. Subtracting $2mL_F(0)e=m A_\lambda^2e$ leaves $(m^3-m)e/12$. Antisymmetry and the $m=0$ case complete the Virasoro relation; commuting with negative multiplication modes extends it from $E$ to every polynomial vector.

The degree shift in [F1] is precisely [F3]'s admissible shift, so $F_\lambda=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}P_d\otimes E$ is admissible. On its degree-$d$ subspace, step 1.1 gives $(L_F(0)-d-\lambda^2/2)^2=0$. Distinct degrees have distinct eigenvalues. If $h\ne d+\lambda^2/2$, then $(d+\lambda^2/2-h)I+\lambda N$ is invertible on that degree, with inverse $c^{-1}I-\lambda c^{-2}N$ where $c=d+\lambda^2/2-h$. Since vectors have only finitely many degree components, the generalized eigenspaces are exactly the stated degree spaces. They have finite dimension $2\dim P_d$ by [F2], and their real parts are bounded below by $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda^2/2)$. This verifies grading restriction in [F3].

If $\lambda\ne0$, on the lowest space $E$ the vector $e_1$ satisfies $(L_F(0)-\lambda^2/2)e_1=\lambda e_0\ne0$ and its second iterate is zero. Thus $L_F(0)$ is not semisimple, and the module is logarithmic by [F4]. If $\lambda=0$, step 1.1 gives $L_F(0)=D$, diagonal on the displayed grading, so the module is ordinary by [F4] and not logarithmic. At $\lambda=1$ the explicit formulas become $a_0=I+N$ and $L_F(0)|_E=I/2+N$. No unproved module-twist, reconstruction-for-modules, classification, or rationality theorem is used.

Let $E=\mathbb C e_0\oplus\mathbb C e_1$, define $Ne_0=0$, $Ne_1=e_0$, and let $A_\lambda=\lambda I+N$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C$. The oscillator module $F_\lambda=F(E,A_\lambda)$ constructed in [[lem-heisenberg-normal-ordered-fields-satisfy-module-jacobi]] is a module over the conformal CFT-type rank-one Heisenberg VOA of central charge $1$. Its conformal modes are

$$L_F(n)=\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}{:}a_k a_{n-k}{:},\qquad L_F(0)=D\otimes I_E+\tfrac12 I_P\otimes A_\lambda^2=D\otimes I_E+\tfrac{\lambda^2}{2}I+\lambda I_P\otimes N,$$

where $D|_{P_d}=dI$. The degree spaces $P_d\otimes E$ give an admissible grading and are exactly the generalized weight spaces of weights $d+\lambda^2/2$, of dimension $2\dim P_d$. Thus $F_\lambda$ is grading-restricted generalized. It is logarithmic exactly when $\lambda\ne0$; at $\lambda=0$ it is ordinary despite its nonsemisimple current zero mode. In particular $F_1$ has $a_0=I+N$ and $L_F(0)|_E=\tfrac12I+N$.

A **logarithmic module** for a conformal vertex algebra of CFT type is a grading-restricted generalized module, as in [[def-grading-restricted-generalized-vertex-module]], on which $L_M(0)$ is not semisimple. Equivalently, some generalized weight space contains $m$ and $h\in\mathbb C$ with $(L_M(0)-h)^r m=0$ and $(L_M(0)-h)^{r-1}m\ne0$ for an integer $r\ge2$. This definition records the Jordan-block condition; it does not assert that a named vertex algebra has such a module or that its module category has any particular tensor, finite-length, or modular property.

derivations.claim: In the ordered basis $e_0,e_1$, $N$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and square zero. Thus $(I+N)^2/2=I/2+N$, giving the two displayed matrices by [F1]. In particular $(L_F(0)-1/2)e_1=e_0\ne0$ and $(L_F(0)-1/2)e_0=0$. These are an actual length-two conformal Jordan chain, not just a nonsemisimple action of an unrelated algebra element.

On a weighted-degree-$d$ monomial $p$, $L_F(0)(p\otimes e_0)=(d+1/2)p\otimes e_0$ and $L_F(0)(p\otimes e_1)=(d+1/2)p\otimes e_1+p\otimes e_0$. The generalized weights are exactly $d+1/2$, with finite spaces $P_d\otimes E$ and lower bound $1/2$, by [F1]. Therefore the module meets every grading restriction and is logarithmic by [F2]. Formally on this pair, exponentiating the nilpotent part terminates and gives $z^{L_F(0)}(p\otimes e_1)=z^{d+1/2}(p\otimes e_1+(\log z)p\otimes e_0)$; this explains the terminology while the module fields themselves remain the ordinary Laurent fields already proved in [F1].
